sections.overview: This Bornean wild betta is restricted to the middle Mahakam drainage in East Kalimantan. It is a member of the albimarginata group and, unlike the bubble-nesting B. brownorum, the male carries the eggs in his mouth.
sections.identification: It is a very small species, with a recorded maximum near 4 cm standard length. Its broad, flattened head recalls a snakehead fish and inspired the name channoides; males develop stronger red and dark coloration than females.
sections.habitat: It lives in shallow, forested acidic streams with blackwater, submerged leaf litter and riparian roots. The known range is exceptionally small, so local habitat changes can affect much of the species at once.
sections.diet: The available accounts describe a small carnivorous fish; small aquatic invertebrates and zooplankton are consistent with its shallow-stream setting. Precise field diet measurements are limited.
sections.behavior: The species breathes with gills and can also use the labyrinth organ to take atmospheric air. Its secretive stream life and mouthbrooding differ from the more conspicuous bubble-nesting behaviour of B. splendens and B. imbellis.
sections.reproduction: Betta channoides is a paternal mouthbrooder: after spawning, the male holds fertilised eggs in his buccal cavity until the young are ready to be released. This reproductive strategy is shared with close B. albimarginata, and contrasts with bubble-nesting species such as B. brownorum.
sections.ecology: Its dependence on forested blackwater habitat makes it sensitive to changes in stream quality and surrounding land use. Compared with the widespread, adaptable B. splendens, its narrow distribution leaves less room for populations to persist elsewhere.
sections.conservation: The 2019 IUCN assessment lists it as Endangered because its extent and area of occupancy are very small, it occurs at few threat-defined locations, and collection for the ornamental trade may contribute to declines. The assessment also identifies habitat pressure in its range.
